items.title: AI-modified home listings are everywhere. What buyers need to know.
items.description: The rise of artificial intelligence is reshaping the real estate industry and regulators are racing to draft rules to draw a line between virtual home staging and false advertising, which is now referred to as housefishing.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[An AI-modified front of a house. Real estate listings are being modified using artificial intelligence, in a practice known as housefishing. (CTV News)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The rise of artificial intelligence is reshaping the real estate industry and regulators are racing to draft rules to draw a line between virtual home staging and false advertising, which is now referred to as housefishing.
items.body:
MONTREAL - The rise of artificial intelligence is reshaping the real estate industry and regulators are racing to draft rules to draw a line between virtual home staging and false advertising, which is now referred to as housefishing.

Homebuyers who browse through listings are finding increasingly well-lit and beautifully decorated properties that were transformed by the click of a finger. At times, it’s hard to tell reality from the dream agents are selling. Now, many buyers and industry players are demanding guidelines.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The Quebec Professional Association of Real Estate Brokers (QPAREB) says the industry has been trying to keep up with how quickly AI is changing the business.

“With AI there are no limits to what we can do,” says QPAREB’s director of brokerage practice Nathalie Bégin. “Right now, we say modified with AI, but we all understand that removing a bag that was left on a counter or adding a pool is not the same thing. So having a clear definition and categories of what has been done would be helpful.”

Marcel Morgenstern, from Ontario, has been scrolling through online sites searching for an investment property for weeks.

“We are used to people staging houses and physically making them look more appealing. But with the dawn of AI, I didn’t realize how much it is being used, or rather, overused in listings these days,” says Morgenstern.

He realized AI’s reach when he started to look more closely at Google Street View images or visited some of the properties. He says that in one particular case, the outside of a building did not match reality. He found several other examples.

“I started to realize that a fresh coat of paint is often not really there,” he says. “One house that I looked at, I knew it needed some work, but we walked in, and I am not being picky here, but it was either a total gut down to the studs or a total tear down.”

The Real Estate Council of Ontario updated its guidelines on the use of AI in the industry in October. Registered agents and brokers are required to disclose that a home has been AI-generated or materially altered. They must also verify the accuracy of AI-generated content against physical facts to ensure that there are no misleading implications about the property’s current condition.

Manitoba has vowed to go further. In a recent throne speech, the government signalled its intention to ban AI-generated images in sales and rental listings.

“When you get taken for a ride and you rent a bunk apartment because you were misled, you are getting ripped off,” said Premier Wab Kinew.

But many in the industry say AI is a useful tool and a total ban is impractical.

“People have a hard time picturing what their home might look like,” says Bégin. “That is why modified photos are useful, it helps clients dream of what it might look like when it has cushions at the right place, it is neat. Many clients see an empty room and can’t figure out what it would look like with furniture.”

In February, a realtor in Terrebonne, Que., had to apologize for using an image edited with AI to add windows, enlarge existing ones, and make the garage door appear larger. The photo included add-ons like a fence and bushes.

The province’s regulator, the OACIQ, has said AI must be used in an ethical and transparent manner, and it has put out some guidelines.

“Fundamentally we want to make sure that the public knows what they are looking at,” says OACIQ Advisor, Regulations and Government Relations Louis E. Romet.

“We want to make sure that the property is represented in a way that is accurate, transparent and faithful to the property in its actual condition. So an example would be that a broker could actually use virtual staging to make a space look brighter and more inviting, but he could never use AI to conceal cracks or add a swimming pool or a second storey to a house.”

He also says inspections are done to ensure compliance, but also that concerned home buyers can call to report problematic situations.

“Should there be concerns regarding professional misbehavior, then the situation could be escalated to the office of the syndicate which could lead to penalties such as fines and license suspensions.”

But many in the province have been discussing more comprehensive rules, and practical ways to implement them.

On some real estate listings sites, labels that an image has been AI-modified are hard to find. Agents say technical restrictions limit the visibility of those notifications and updates are in the works.

The QPAREB also says it would like to see categories of modifications. For instance, some AI-modifications could be labelled as projects.

“If a house is in a neighbourhood where all the houses have a pool, but not this one, and we know buyers will want a pool, then we might want to show what that would look like with an AI image,” says Bégin. “But the responsibilities would not stop there. The broker would have to determine if that would comply with localization certificate, that it would fit, whether a fence would have to be changed for instance.”

She says new rules would benefit buyers, sellers and brokers.

“It’s essential that people can have access to see all pictures including those without modifications before they visit and understand what they will see,” says Bégin. “Or else there will be disappointment when someone walks through the door, and that is not good for anyone.”

Morgenstern says that kind of let-down is a poor sales technique.

“It reminds me of that saying that in sales or in service. You are supposed to under promise and over deliver, this is the exact opposite of that,” he says.

While he hasn’t closed a deal yet, Morgenstern says he may have found a property he likes.

“That one was not AI-enhanced, I can tell you that. It looked exactly like I had seen online when I drove up to it and when we walked into it,” he says. “To me, if you are hiding something or trying to make something better than what it actually is, then I have my doubts right off the bat.”

items.title: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20 per cent and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during an event to announce new tariffs in the Rose Garden at the White House, April 2, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Mark Schiefelbein</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20 per cent and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
items.body:
WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration announced a set of broad new tariffs Wednesday on imports from China, the European Union, Taiwan and 11 other countries in response to their alleged overproduction of factory goods that have disadvantaged American firms.

The new tariffs are also intended to help replace the revenue lost after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in February that U.S. President Donald Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.

Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, said that “many of our trading partners have adopted ... market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”

The proposed duties range from 15 per cent to 35 per cent and could cover roughly three-fifths of U.S. imports, though the administration also proposed exemptions for products such as semiconductors and other high-tech goods from Taiwan and South Korea, which are crucial to the artificial intelligence buildout.

While sweeping, the tariffs largely replace those first imposed last April and should have a modest impact on inflation and growth, economists said.

The duties “were widely expected, are relatively small, and would return us roughly to where we were earlier in the year,” Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics, said.

Yet the announcement demonstrates the Trump administration’s willingness to continue imposing tariffs even after voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. About two-thirds of voters said that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.

Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year’s tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.

Greer said he did not expect the tariffs to rattle the global economy.

“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this -- they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

The administration will next seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing Jan. 25, suggesting the duties won’t take effect until February or March.

Tariffs may be here to stay despite electoral sweep

Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the Finance Committee next year, said he will “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”

“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”

Still, any effort to overturn them faces steep odds, even after Democrats take control of both chambers in January. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

After roughly two years of seemingly arbitrary tariffs imposed on a range of trading partners from Canada and Europe to Brazil, the duties announced Wednesday reflect a key goal of Trump’s trade policy: pushing back against subsidized factories overseas that allegedly flood global markets with cheap goods that undercut U.S. manufacturers.

The small business advocacy group We Pay the Tariffs, which urged Congress to roll back all tariffs after the election, slammed Wednesday’s maneuver.

“Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses,” Dan Anthony, executive director of the group, said in a prepared statement. “Customers can’t afford more price increases, but small businesses can’t afford to absorb tariffs on top tariffs either.”

Brazil and China will face some of the biggest hits

The levies will be imposed pursuant to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.

A senior Trump administration official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.

Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after trade talks stalled. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10 per cent tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

For some Chinese goods, the new 20 per cent tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45 per cent.

Vietnam also faces a 20 per cent tariff, pending finalization of trade talks, the USTR said on Wednesday. U.S. imports from India would be taxed at 17 per cent if it reaches a trade deal with the U.S., and 20 per cent if not.

The U.S. and China last year reached a trade truce that is set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for US$30 billion worth of Chinese goods in line with the truce.

Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China’s purchases of American agricultural products could come up again.

On Wednesday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs again stated its opposition while calling for the U.S. to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Williams of Capital Economics noted that China was often singled out as a target Wednesday, a development he said was at odds with the administration’s “apparent lack of concern about allegations that semiconductor export restrictions have been circumvented,” a reference to the controversy surrounding Nvidia and whether Chinese firms have accessed its most advanced chips.

But it “signals that significant parts of the U.S. government remain hawkish on China,” he added.

Other analysts criticized the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour,” he added.

The tariffs won’t stack on top of other taxes on cars and steel

Goldman Sachs calculates that the proposal would return most tariffs on the affected countries to where they were before the U.S. Supreme Court ruling in February. Goldman also estimates that if implemented, the import taxes would increase the overall U.S. tariff rate from 7.8 per cent to 9.2 per cent and have “a very small incremental impact” on inflation.

The new import taxes are targeted to specific products and would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.

Nor would they stack on top of levies of 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.

Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. Two other countries face pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.

The USTR posted extensive reports on each country’s alleged unfair trade practices, with the report on China reaching 456 pages. The Section 301 law requires specific analysis of each country’s trade practices to pass legal muster.

Wednesday’s duties will likely face legal challenges, as Trump’s forced labor tariffs already have. At least some of the forced labor duties could be overturned, said Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer and former official in Trump’s first term who also served in the Biden administration, because the USTR didn’t provide extensive evidence for each of the 60 countries affected by those duties.

The Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

By Christopher Rugaber, Aamer Madhani and Josh Boak

AP writers Mae Anderson in New York City and Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.

items.title: Wall street recovers most early losses as pullback in AI stocks eases
items.description: Stocks on Wall Street closed moderately lower after another punishing pullback in AI stocks lost momentum, reversing much of the market’s losses.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Fearless Girl statue stands in front of the New York Stock Exchange in New York's Financial District on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (AP Photo/Peter Morgan, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Stocks on Wall Street closed moderately lower after another punishing pullback in AI stocks lost momentum, reversing much of the market’s losses.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Stocks on Wall Street closed moderately lower Wednesday after another punishing pullback in AI stocks lost momentum as the day went on, reversing much of the market’s losses.

The S&P 500 index fell 0.3 per cent after having been down as much as 3.2 per cent earlier in the day. The Nasdaq composite finished 0.6 per cent lower. At one point, it had been down as much as 4.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3 per cent.

The market pared its losses even as a report raised more worries about high inflation and as President Donald Trump plans to escalate the U.S. trade war with major trading partners.

AI stocks lost ground for a second day following Monday’s relief rally over the surprise reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Stocks have been generally falling since setting an all-time high last month as worries grow that AI stock prices have grown unjustifiably high.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

The market turnaround came as some of the biggest tech companies bounced back from steep drops. Nvidia, which was down more than nine per cent at one point, closed with a 3.9 per cent loss.

Broadcom, which had dropped more than six per cent, ended just 0.1 per cent lower, while Microsoft came back from a more than 3 per cent slide to finish down 1.2 per cent.

There were some gainers among tech stocks: Meta climbed 3.4 per cent and Salesforce rose 2 per cent.

Gains in financial services stocks also helped temper the market’s losses. Visa rose 1.8 per cent, Mastercard gained 1.9 per cent and American Express rose 1.2 per cent.

Anthropic bounced back from an early drop to close with a 1.1 per cent gain. Still, since soaring to US$115 per share on the day it became the first major frontier lab to go public, Anthropic shares have tumbled by about 28 per cent.

Roughly three quarters of the stocks in the S&P 500 rose, although the pullback in technology stocks kept the index in the red.

Technology companies, particularly those focused on AI, have large market values that give them a dominant influence over whether major indexes rise or fall. Nvidia is among the most valuable companies on Wall Street and its surge on Monday led a tech sector rally. It is now one of the biggest weights pushing the market lower.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

The S&P 500 index is down 5.2 per cent for November, after losing some ground in October and September.

“At this point, between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn’t look like the Santa Claus Rally is in store for us this year,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, in a research note.

Questions about Nvidia’s corporate governance, as well as the influence of a U.S. president who owns millions of dollars’ worth of shares in the company, have added to concerns surrounding the artificial intelligence sector. Relief over Huang’s return as CEO is fading because of worries that AI might not produce enough profit to justify the large investments and stock values.

That dynamic is running up against stubbornly high inflation. The latest update on inflation showed that prices rose at a more aggressive 3.8 per cent rate in October from the same period last year, and followed a 3.6 per cent rate in September. The data is from the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation, the personal consumption expenditures price index.

Aside from potentially stifling economic growth, high inflation could mean higher interest rates, with the Fed likely to raise its benchmark interest rate at its December policy meeting to try to tame inflation. The rate of inflation is well above the central bank’s target of 2 per cent.

The economy has been resilient, though, even as inflation squeezes households and businesses and consumers grow increasingly anxious about spending and finances. The government said that the economy grew even faster in the July-September quarter than previously estimated, with growth revised upward to a 4.3 per cent annual rate, the fastest in three years.

Much of the spending that is driving the economy, though, has been from large tech firms building out AI infrastructure and from upper-income households. There are signs poorer Americans are relying more on credit to sustain their spending.

Higher oil prices, fueled by the U.S. war with Iran and its impact on the world’s oil supply, have also contributed to inflation. The price of a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 3.5 per cent to settle at US$94.61 on Wednesday. The price has swung between US$72 and US$114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Energy companies mostly gained ground Wednesday, including a 1.1 per cent rise for Chevron.

The wide-ranging and often uncertain U.S. trade conflict with much of the world also added to rising costs. The U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, the European Union and other trading partners after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down broader tariffs that were set last year.

Businesses tend to pass along some or all of the cost of tariffs to consumers. Anger over stubbornly high prices was a factor in pushing voters to punish Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.87 per cent from 4.91 per cent late Tuesday.

Markets fell throughout Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi lost 6.2 per cent as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9 per cent and SK Hynix plummeted 11.1 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 per cent. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8 per cent.

U.S. financial markets will be closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. On Friday, the stock market will close at 1:00 p.m. Eastern, and the bond market will close at 2:00 p.m. Eastern.

Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press

Business reporter Elaine Lai and economics writer Christopher Rugaber contributed to this report.

items.title: Too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, a new report finds
items.description: A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government’s quest to recruit highly educated, highly specialized workers from abroad.

items._ogDesc: A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government’s quest to recruit highly educated, highly specialized workers from abroad.
items.body:
OTTAWA — A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government’s quest to recruit highly educated, highly specialized workers from abroad.

The Institute for Canadian Citizenship’s annual report — “Selected But Neglected” — argues the government needs to do more work on foreign credential recognition in key fields like health care to ensure immigrants who are courted for their qualifications can actually put them to work.

The institute projects half of the 380,000 permanent residents admitted to Canada next year will have a university education, but only 36 per cent of those people will have jobs that make use of their education and qualifications over the next 20 years.

Almost half of those with university degrees — 47 per cent — will hold jobs below their education levels, and almost one in five will leave Canada over the next 20 years, the institute says.

Heather Barnabe, the institute’s chief operating officer, told a news conference in Ottawa on Wednesday the problem is particularly dire in the health care sector.

“Just 38 per cent of 2027 immigrants with health care training are projected to work in a job befitting their education by 2035,” she said.

“If these immigrants experienced the same qualification-matched employment rate as their Canadian-born peers, over 2,000 extra health professionals would be providing urgently needed care to us and our loved ones.”

Daniel Bernhard, citizenship institute CEO, said some provinces have worked out ways to recognize immigrants’ professional credentials. He pointed to a program in Nova Scotia which allows immigrant doctors to work under the supervision of a Canadian physician as their competency is assessed.

Bernhard said while it’s important to verify credentials and work experience to ensure they meet Canadian standards, some provinces and territories put up too many roadblocks.

“Colleges have … I would call them discriminatory practices when it comes to immigrant professionals coming in. They do things like make you take a separate English or French test, then they take two years to process your paperwork. Then when it’s done, they say, ‘Your English or French test expired, you’ve got to do it all over again,’” he said.

“All Canadians expect, rightly so, that these professions be conducted by people who are qualified and who can do so safely. I don’t think anybody objects to that. But there are faster ways to do it.”

A Medical Council of Canada spokesperson said in an emailed statement the council also worries that too many internationally trained physicians are unable to practice in Canada.

The spokesperson said the council is working with regulators, governments and other parties to find ways to make licensing pathways more clear for physicians trained abroad. 

The Medical Council of Canada is not a licensing body but it works to ensure national standards for verifying physician credentials and assessing their competency.

Census data from 2016 and 2021 shows 88 per cent of Canadian-born working-age people are in jobs that match their education levels, while just 62 per cent of immigrants can say the same.

The institute cites a 2019 RBC report that estimates closing the labour gap between immigrant and Canadian-born workers could have boosted Canada’s gross domestic product by about $50 billion at the time. The bank’s economists found immigrants were earning about 10 per cent less than their Canadian-born peers.

The report also calls on the government to do more to track how many immigrants are underemployed and how many eventually leave Canada for other opportunities.

This report comes at a time when the debate over Canada’s immigration policy is heating up.

Claiming higher immigration will put too much pressure on health services and the housing market, the Conservative opposition tabled a motion in the House of Commons this week to block the government’s plan for permanent resident admissions in 2027.

That motion was defeated Wednesday, with the Liberals, NDP and Green Party voting against it.

Bernhard said while there are real factors driving public skepticism of immigration around the world, allowing qualified people to work is a solution to pressures on public services.

“So if you’re feeling squeezed at the hospital, if you are feeling squeezed with an overcrowded classroom, and you are worried about more people coming in, then presumably we can agree that anybody who’s already here who can help to make that situation better does a service for the whole country,” he said.

The government does grant preferred immigration access to those with higher education and more work experience in high-demand fields like the trades, medicine and research.

The report’s methodology uses a combination of Statistics Canada, census and long-term immigration data to make its projections.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

items.title: PM Carney says Pentagon’s complaints about Canada haven’t come up in Trump talks
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Pentagon’s recent complaints about Canada’s defence spending have not come up in his conversations with U.S. President Donald Trump.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks with reporters as he makes his way to caucus on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Pentagon’s recent complaints about Canada’s defence spending have not come up in his conversations with U.S. President Donald Trump.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Pentagon’s recent complaints about Canada’s defence spending have not come up in his conversations with U.S. President Donald Trump.

On Monday, the Pentagon released what it called a “fact sheet” claiming Canada’s defence spending has limited its ability to contribute to the protection of North America.

Asked about those complaints on his way into the Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday, Carney said Trump hasn’t brought up those concerns with him.

“I can assure you that in my discussions with the president the United States, we’re focused on conflict resolution around the world and he has not raised issues such as has been reported recently,” Carney said.

The prime minister said Canada is taking responsibility for its own defence. He said Canada is on the front lines in Europe through Operation Reassurance in Latvia and is engaging with NATO partners to secure the Arctic and the Far North.

Carney also said Canada is making “historic investments” in its military and getting members of the armed forces the pay they deserve.

Under U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Trump administration has taken symbolic steps to upend the long-standing bilateral defence relationship between Canada and the United States.

Hegseth last week issued a classified memo imposing restrictions on military co-operation with Canada on think-tanks and socializing.

Defence Minister David McGuinty said Tuesday he can’t “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s recent criticism of Canada’s defence spending.

“The amount of co-operation that we are pursuing together under Norad has not changed. What we are doing together at NATO has not changed,” McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa. “Our military-to-military co-operation has not changed.”

Stephen Fuhr, secretary of state for defence procurement, suggested Wednesday that the Pentagon’s “briefing books haven’t been updated recently.” He cited Canada hitting NATO’s two per cent spending target earlier this year and its plans to buy new submarines, radar units and aircraft.

“Our readiness has been not where we want it to be, and we all acknowledge that, but we’re making great progress and changing it. We’re buying new capabilities, we’re moving faster, more people are joining the Canadian Forces,” he told reporters before the caucus meeting Wednesday.

“If we were to react to every single thing that came out of the United States, we’d have a headache. I don’t think they either know or appreciate how fast we’re moving.”

A senior U.S. Department of Defense official said Hegseth’s memo was intended to ensure a unified objective during engagements with Canada. It does not affect military operations.

The Trump administration official briefed a small group of Canadian journalists Monday on background in order to speak more candidly about Canada-U.S. relations.

The official, who said the Pentagon is looking for Canada to commit to a realistic approach focused on military efficiency, cited the F-35 review.

The Liberal government has yet to reach a decision on its full order of F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed Martin — which Pentagon officials have cited as a source of frustration. Canada has committed to buy 16 of the aircraft, but the decision on the remainder of the planned 88-aircraft order has been the subject of a political review for more than a year.

On Wednesday, Fuhr rejected the idea that the Pentagon was putting pressure on Ottawa to purchase the jets.

He said Canada is still buying military equipment from the United States but is also diversifying into other markets and spending more of its defence dollars at home.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre told reporters after question period on Wednesday that Hegseth should not dictate how Canada spends its defence dollars.

But he also took issue with how the Liberals have been doling out defence spending and claimed the government is lining the pockets of lobbyists and corporations rather than helping military personnel.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa and Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items.body:
OTTAWA — The federal government is imposing import limits and tariffs on some canned vegetable products after the Canadian International Trade Tribunal found that increased imports of canned vegetable goods are causing serious injury to domestic producers.

A Department of Finance news release says the government is imposing a tariff rate quota set at 13,000,000 kg for the first year, and a tariff of 50 per cent on imports above quota.

Imports under the quota limit will not be subject to this tariff and the news release says the quota volume will increase gradually to just over 13,500,000 kg, while the above-quota tariff rate will decrease to 40 per cent.

The news release says the tariff rate quota will be in effect from Dec. 1, to June 17, 2029, and will apply to imports from all countries except Mexico, Chile, Israel, Colombia, Korea, Panama, Peru and some developing countries.

Portions of the quota have been reserved for imports from the United States, the European Union and Thailand, the release says.

The release says the government is also directing the tribunal to launch a product exclusion process for certain canned vegetables early next year, which will allow parties to request exemptions for some imports.

items._ogDesc: Federal Liberals, including Mark Carney, are defending the speed at which their major projects bill passed through a House committee — a process one opposition MP called 'brutal.'
items.body:
OTTAWA — Federal Liberals, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, are defending the speed at which their major projects bill passed through a House of Commons committee -- a process one opposition MP called “inhumane.”

The committee reviewing Bill C-39 spent more than 100 hours debating it over seven days before wrapping up on Monday. The Liberals used their majority to accept only minor amendments to the sweeping bill, which is meant to fast-track approvals for major projects, cut their review times and create zones of “national interest” to pre-approve certain types of projects.

It also proposes major changes to collective bargaining, including the use of more federal mediation to get deals done and repair relationships between unions and businesses.

Opposition MPs said they aren’t taking issue with the long hours -- which they acknowledged are part of the job -- they argued a longer period of debate with some breaks would have allowed them to provide better oversight.

MPs, staff and witnesses often sat in committee until close to midnight over the seven days they spent reviewing the bill. The committee logged back-to-back 15-hour days on Saturday and Sunday.

“It was really excessive. I would say it was on the line of being inhumane,” Bloc Quebecois MP Gabriel Ste-Marie said in French.

“After 15 hours, we’re aren’t as effective anymore to find the right words to get our point across.”

“I would have preferred for there to be breaks because … what goes on actually in the committee, there’s hours of prep,” Conservative MP Phil Lawrence told The Canadian Press on Wednesday.

“So it’s nice to be able to, after a couple of hours, go back to your office review it, and you see what changes have been made, and you can have a little bit more substance.

“Give us at least the evening to review, to change, to sub-amend. Because that reflection time can often make the bill better. It also gives time for the witnesses, the officials, to recap and recover.”

On Tuesday, Manitoba Conservative MP Branden Leslie called the committee process “pretty brutal.”

“I mean, I’ll be very frank, this is our job. But the witnesses that had to sit at the end of that table and take questions for hours and hours on end, yeah, it was pretty brutal on them, as well as all the support staff,” he said.

“My entire time in Parliament, and I have been here over seven years, I’ve never seen anything like this,” said NDP MP Heather McPherson.

“Nobody’s at their best after 15-hour days, on and on and on … Nobody is doing the work that we need to be able to do. It’s impossible.”

Committee chair James Maloney defended the long hours spent reviewing the bill, although he also acknowledged he’d never seen that happen before.

“Everybody was on board with it. The longer it went, the longer it would have gone. And once you get a little momentum in the committee, it’s good to keep going,” said Maloney, who also serves as the Liberal caucus chair.

“I was tasked with chairing the committee and I decided on the schedule in consultation with all the members, I might add. So there’s no surprise to anyone, if they’re being candid about it. It was my decision.”

While Ste-Marie denied the claim that MPs were consulted on the schedule, he also said Maloney was a “gentleman” throughout the process.

“I don’t think it was his choice to have those hours. I’m convinced that it was an order from the government to have those hours. I have a lot of respect for Mr. Maloney,” Ste-Marie said in French.

“The message was clear: ‘We’re going to fatigue you, we’re going to burn you out, and we’re going to come out ahead, regardless if we respect the staff who are there.’ It’s disrespectful of the democratic process.”

Carney has described the bill as his government’s most consequential piece of economic legislation.

When asked if the pace at which the committee reviewed the bill was excessive, Carney replied, “Absolutely not.”

“I think it’s a mistake to count days as opposed to hours spent on the actual clause-by-clause review,” he told reporters.

“I want to salute all members of the committee, obviously members of the government caucus, but all members of the committee for the time they put in.

“They, didn’t get to spend quality time with their family on the weekend, at various events. Some people came in, missed birthdays and other things, in order to move forward.”

The Senate has started its review on the bill, even though it has yet to pass third and final reading in the House of Commons.

The Senate committee has begun hearing from a list witnesses which already exceeds the number of witnesses who presented to the House committee.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

items.body:
The sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks is drawing comparisons with the dot-com bust. Sharp rebounds have interrupted the decline.

BNN Bloomberg spoke with Dan Niles, founder and portfolio manager at Niles Investment Management, about which businesses he sees as most vulnerable if the AI boom cools.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

Key Takeaways

  • Niles says U.S. ballot measures limiting data centre construction and restrictions on Chinese companies training AI models abroad could weigh on demand for AI chips and computing capacity.
  • Niles says a price war between OpenAI and Anthropic has slowed their combined revenue growth and widened losses, while cheaper open-weight models are adding to pricing pressure.
  • Niles expects large language models to become interchangeable for many users, with more value going to the apps that select and use them.
  • Niles sees SoftBank and the specialized cloud providers it finances as vulnerable if big tech companies bring more computing in-house, while established businesses could cushion companies such as Microsoft and Amazon.
  • Niles sees the U.S. Federal Reserve as a bigger near-term risk because higher borrowing costs could make the AI buildout more expensive to finance.

Read the full transcript below:

LINDSAY: Equities around the world are lower today as the AI trade faces further pressure. What’s driving the latest wave of investor jitters? Joining us now for more on all of that is Dan Niles, founder and portfolio manager at Niles Investment Management. It’s great to have you join us. Thanks for taking the time.

DAN: My pleasure, Lindsay.

LINDSAY: So a lot of investors are drawing comparisons between today’s AI boom and the dot-com bubble in 2000. Obviously, there’s some significant differences in revenues and valuations. But are there any parallels that suggest we could be heading down a similar path, do you think?

DAN: Yeah, I mean, there is, and I’ve been talking about this really since, you know, late June. In that you have a great industrial revolution, and if you go back and you look at all the big ones, right? Whether it’s canals, railroads, electricity or dot-com, you have a tremendous amount of companies chasing the same big revolution because they know if they’re the last company standing, they’re going to make an incredible amount of money. And so, if you go back to the dot-com period, you had a good five years plus of expansion, but then you ended up with Nasdaq going down 70 per cent and the S&P 49 per cent over two and a half years. And if you fast-forward to today, what — what’s really changed? Well, what’s changed is we had the midterm elections in the United States. Forty out of 41 ballot initiatives to halt or slow down data centre construction passed in local initiatives. And so, if you don’t have anywhere to put this hardware or chips, how are you going to make, you know, these estimates that people have? And then the second part is if you cut China off from being able to train on data centres outside of China, well, that was a lot of demand, and we’ve already seen some data points come out, which we can get into if you want, on demand already starting to fall off because China is getting cut off from external training capacity.

LINDSAY: Yeah, tell us about — more about that. What are you seeing right now in those data points?

DAN: Well, I’ll give you one example that came out recently that sort of got lost in all this Jensen noise. But Datasection is a publicly traded neocloud in Japan. They came out and cut their revenue forecasts for the fiscal year ending in March of ’27 by 89 per cent because they didn’t give the name, but people pretty much know it’s Tencent, which is obviously a Chinese company. They can’t train outside into Japan, and that’s what’s occurring with them, but you’ve also had some data points coming out like Nebius, which is a neocloud as well, and this was, you know, back a few weeks ago. But they also guided below the Street, so you’ve got this stuff going on that tells you you’ve got an issue. And at the same time, if you look, if you take a hard look at Anthropic and OpenAI combined, you can see that their revenue growth is slowing because they’re in a price war with each other, right? Their revenue growth combined sequentially was 75 per cent in Q2. That dropped below 50 per cent in Q3. Reason is OpenAI was starting to cut prices to try to get back market share that they had lost to Anthropic, but then you look at the losses. The losses went up by a half a billion dollars from Q2 to Q3, so you go, revenue growth is slowing, losses are going up, and then you have open weight sitting on top of this, which, you know, you can do what the highest-end models for Anthropic or OpenAI do for a tenth of the cost. And with Jensen back, that’s one of the negatives for those two companies, is he’s a big proponent of open weight. And I think open weight is good for all of us, right? Like, you and I, Lindsay, aren’t going to go try to cure cancer, right? We don’t need the highest-end models from OpenAI or Anthropic. We can use something a lot cheaper to get what we need done, and that’s what open weight gives you. But that’s also pressure on the revenues and profits you can generate.

LINDSAY: I’m sure you saw what happened with SoftBank overnight, shares tumbling to its lowest in over a year. It’s such a major player in tech investing and lending. Do you worry that this could turn into something even bigger than just a tech sell-off? Maybe even create the kind of credit problems that triggered the global financial crisis?

DAN: Yeah, I mean, I think SoftBank. Well, let me put you this way. If you look at neoclouds, neoclouds are overflow capacity for the big guys, right? Microsoft, Google, they’ll go ahead and contract out with these neoclouds for excess capacity. Well, SoftBank goes ahead and finances all these neoclouds. Well, what happens when excess capacity turns into too much capacity? Well, the big guys will go ahead and say, you know what, I don’t need that excess capacity anymore. I’m going to do this all internally. And Microsoft, as an example of that, has been very clear that they want to build internally if they can, and they’re just using neoclouds as an example. They were, you know, over 70 per cent of revenues at CoreWeave, as an example of this, at one point. So back to your question on SoftBank. If that does occur, I think all the neoclouds — you know, a good portion of them, let’s say 80 per cent — go to zero. They won’t exist anymore, and SoftBank’s just going to get absolutely crushed in that process. So SoftBank’s a name that I haven’t liked because they’ve levered themselves up to this trade, and, you know, this is a bigger investment in the U.S. economy than if you combine all the big investments in the 1990s of electricity, you know, highways and the internet. This is bigger than all of them combined. So it is eventually — and, you know, it’s going to burst, right? It has to because all of these companies know they’re overinvesting. They’ve been very clear on the fact that they’re overinvesting, and so when this does break, you’re going to have a lot of carnage underneath it. And — but by the way, let’s not forget about the Fed, which I think is a bigger problem in the near term, because this has a lot of similarities to 2018 in that money is getting more expensive. Right, debt costs are going up if you want to borrow to finance this AI trade. Obviously, Anthropic broke its IPO. I’m not surprised. I put out a note on that saying I doubt — you know, I had doubts whether it was going to be able to hold its IPO price. And so debt’s getting more expensive. Equity is getting more expensive if you can get it. And then you have the Fed raising rates. They skipped the rate hike right before the midterms, for, in my opinion, political reasons. They’re going to have to get more aggressive on the other side, and so this has shades of 2018 where the Fed was raising while global growth was slowing, and you had Trump 1.0 in a trade war with China, and the S&P drew down 20 per cent. I’m hoping that that’s not what occurs this time, from peak to trough. But, you know, you have to keep that in the back of your mind that that’s possible given this confluence of events.

LINDSAY: Do you see a future where companies can build entire business models around LLMs, or do you think this is a feature that’s really going to be commoditized?

DAN: No, I think so. The way I’ve said it is this. LLMs are going to be commoditized, right? So what you and I are probably going to do in the future, Lindsay, is we’ll say, “Hey, Siri, go do this for me.” Or if you’re on, you know, an Android phone, you’ll interact through that. If you’re in the corporate environment, right, you’re probably going to end up using Microsoft, and you’re going to use Copilot, and you’re going to ask it to go do something for you. That will pick the model it uses, whether it’s OpenAI, Anthropic or a cheap open-source model that’s out there, Nemotron from Nvidia or whatever it is, and you won’t even know what you’re using underneath it. And so the model layer, OpenAI, Anthropics of the world, they’re just going to get commoditized, and you’re going to be ambivalent to what’s actually going on underneath the hood. And so I think those companies are going to have a big issue going forward, and the value is going to accrue above the model layer for that reason. I mean, the — the thing I always say is, right? You don’t need a Ferrari to go to the corner store to get milk.

DAN: Right. A Ford will work just fine, and the open-weight models for the 95 per cent of us like you and me that aren’t going to try to cure cancer, that’ll work just fine, which will commoditize that model layer.

LINDSAY: Despite all the selling we’ve been seeing across AI over the last couple of weeks, the hyperscalers have held up pretty well. What do you think the market is trying to tell us here?

DAN: Well, that’s a fantastic question, Lindsay. So this goes back to the question you asked earlier around SoftBank. So let’s — let’s go back to the tech bubble, right? During the tech bubble, you had over 1,000 internet companies go to zero, but you had companies survive like Amazon. So if you look at the hyperscalers, they’ve got other businesses, right? Microsoft, obviously, software. Google’s got search. Meta’s got a great moat with social, which isn’t going to get replaced by AI, right? You and I don’t go to Instagram or, you know, Reels, etc., to search. We go there to be entertained, and so in — Amazon obviously has e-commerce, right? So they’ve got other businesses. So even if you have an implosion in the AI trade in terms of what you can rent out capacity for, or these model layers getting commoditized, they’re going to survive. They’re going to be fine. Now, it doesn’t mean their stocks aren’t going to get killed. Much like Amazon stock. If you go back to 2000 to 2002, from peak to trough, the stock went down 90 per cent. Ninety. Obviously, it survived. It didn’t go to zero. So what I’m trying to say is, you’re going to see an issue with these — with these names also. It’s just relative to other names that could go to zero, which is neoclouds. They’re going to get through this. They’re going to be fine, and their base businesses are massive cash flow generators. Right. The only reason that some of them have gone cash flow negative is because they’ve been spending so much on AI. But if the AI, you know, growth rate slows — and by the way, that’s what happened during the internet bubble breaking too, is the internet went from doubling every three months to then it was doubling every year. Right? It didn’t stop growing in 2001 and 2002. It doubled each of those years as well. But that growth rate slowed down quite a bit, and that’s why you had the implosion of these other names while the strong ones kind of survived, and that’s what the hyperscalers are, right? They’re the strong names that got other businesses that will survive.

LINDSAY: I want to ask you about Nvidia as well, because it was your largest holding as of Monday. The stock ripped more than 30 per cent after Jensen Huang’s return was announced. Is it still your biggest position, or did you manage to take some profits before yesterday’s reversal?

DAN: Yeah, I mean, I said on Monday in a different interview that I was selling. So, you know, there’s — so this actually gets to an important point. If you go back to the tech bubble, the Nasdaq went down 78 per cent from peak to trough over two and a half years. You had seven rallies in the Nasdaq, though, that averaged 25 per cent each. Those 25 per cent gains happened over the space of two months, because, you know, investors want to believe, right? Because I’m sure you have people come on your show and say, “Oh, it’s a great buying opportunity,” and, you know, AI is going to be so much bigger 10 years from now. You got to buy it. They were saying the same thing because I was on Wall Street as a sell-side guy back during that period. It was the same kind of thing. It’s not like the internet went away in ’01, ’02. It kept growing, but you had these vicious rallies, and you wanted to use those rallies to sell. And then when you get to a period of time — and the reason it was my biggest position was on the Friday before, and, you know, I post these things on X. Friday before, I was like, well, everything is massively oversold. We’re probably going to get reflex rally on Monday, just based on the models I have and what they show as oversold levels, and then you end up with these vicious rallies underneath it. And the tricky part is going up. You know, when do I sell? But as you rightly pointed out, right? Nvidia is my largest position. Do I want to own it up 30-something per cent that day, or do I want to be selling? Of course, I want to be selling.

DAN: You know, unless you’re a dyed-in-the-wool optimist and you’re not actually paying attention to some of the data points.

LINDSAY: For sure. Okay, we got to leave it there. We’re out of time. Dan Niles, a founder and portfolio manager at Niles Investment Management. Appreciate you sticking around for two blocks. Thanks so much.

DAN: My pleasure, Lindsay. Happy Thanksgiving.

items.description: Nova Scotia’s new Liberal leader is calling on her former colleagues in the Progressive Conservative government to put a planned AI data centre project in Cape Breton on hold.

THE CANADIAN PRESS/Lyndsay Armstrong]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Lyndsay Armstrong</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Nova Scotia’s new Liberal leader is calling on her former colleagues in the Progressive Conservative government to put a planned AI data centre project in Cape Breton on hold.
items.body:
HALIFAX — Nova Scotia’s new Liberal leader is calling on her former colleagues in the Progressive Conservative government to put a planned AI data centre project in Cape Breton on hold.

Becky Druhan said the project should be paused until government establishes regulations to protect communities, electricity bills, water supply and the environment.

“Ambition needs to be matched with good judgment. Announcing a big project is one thing, making sure it’s a good deal for Nova Scotians is another,” she said during a news conference Wednesday.

“That’s where the Houston government approach, particularly with the Point Tupper data centre development, falls woefully short,” Druhan added.

Premier Tim Houston has repeatedly said electricity bills will not rise as a result of the AI data centre, and that communities, water and the environment will be protected.

In a Sept. 23 Facebook post, he shared a list of requirements that he says a company interested in building a data centre in Nova Scotia must meet.

This list included meeting or exceeding the federal government’s responsible AI data centre development standards, which are not binding, and requiring that a project provide a direct financial return to Nova Scotians.

Druhan said protections need to be clear, enforceable and backed by law. “Handshakes aren’t protections,” she said. “A post on Facebook is no substitute for regulations.”

Houston’s office issued an emailed statement Wednesday afternoon saying it’s “interesting” that Nova Scotia’s Liberals are at odds with the federal Liberals when it comes to AI data centres.

“We can both protect our environment and grow our economy. The Mark Carney Liberals recognize that and have been supporting this project every step of the way,” reads the statement.

The premier’s office did not answer a question about whether he would be willing to implement new regulations to address concerns raised by Druhan.

Last month, the premier said it’s not clear to him if any new legislation is needed to manage AI data centres.

“Do we want to do a piece of legislation for every business that sets up in Nova Scotia? Probably not. I mean, we’ve got to be realistic about these things. We have guidelines. We have approval processes. And they’ll be followed,” the premier said Oct. 28.

Druhan was previously the justice minister and attorney general in Houston’s cabinet, but resigned in the fall of 2025 after expressing concerns about the government’s leadership. She joined the Liberals in May and was elected leader over the weekend.

She said Liberals want to return to the legislature to debate and solidify data centre safeguards as soon as possible. The Nova Scotia NDP previously called on the government to reconvene the legislature and debate the topic.

EverWind Fuels announced last month its plans to build and own a 95-megawatt, 18,600-square-metre data centre at a cost of $8 billion, with another $2 billion planned for wind farms to power the operation.

American artificial intelligence firm Anthropic signed a 20-year lease for what would be the company’s first Canadian AI data centre.

Druhan said the need for strict protections is particularly important given the ongoing tension between Canada and U.S. President Donald Trump, and his new threat to tax American companies that build data centres outside of the U.S.

Trump threatened Friday to impose “a tremendous tax,” saying the U.S. could fall behind China in the artificial intelligence race as growing political backlash threatens to put the brakes on American data centre development.

“We’re not going to allow companies to build data centres in other countries,” Trump said. “If they do that, they can. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.”

Druhan said Anthropic could be affected by Trump’s tax threats, which reinforces her concerns about the project’s viability and the potential financial risk associated with the planned development.

EverWind said Nova Scotia’s existing regulatory framework establishes extensive requirements around industrial water withdrawals, environmental protection, electricity generation and more.

Laurel Munroe, a spokesperson for Nova Scotia-based EverWind, said in a statement that the company is subject to various legally enforceable regulatory and contractual obligations, not “voluntary commitments or corporate promises.”

“EverWind is fully committed to transparency and accountability and will always comply with established legislative and regulatory requirements, but Nova Scotians deserve an accurate understanding of the significant protections already in place,” Munroe said.

Druhan also criticized the government for not holding consultations with Nova Scotians until after the data centre project had been announced, and for co-hosting the virtual sessions with the company behind the project.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

Lyndsay Armstrong, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Governor Tiff Macklem’s hawkish speech has BMO calling for a December rate hike to 2.75%, right as the Bank of Canada revives its old CPIX measure
items.body:
Canada’s central bank wasn’t discussing rate hikes, but it left a loud and clear message. Bank of Canada (BoC) Governor Tiff Macklem delivered a hawkish speech in Toronto this week, all but confirming rate hikes. BMO Capital Markets now expects the BoC to hike its key policy rate at its December meeting, after the Governor stated the economy no longer needs stimulus.

Bank of Canada Expected To Hike In December, Says BMO

After the latest comments from the BoC Governor, BMO sees a 25-basis-point hike in December. That would leave the policy rate at 2.75%, the mid-point of the neutral policy range, where monetary policy neither provides stimulus nor becomes restrictive. The hawkish tone appears to have surprised BMO, which noted the Governor didn’t address any economic weakness.

“Governor Macklem’s speech in Toronto reinforced the Bank of Canada’s recent hawkish messaging. He omitted any mention of the recent run of soft data, and reiterated worries about spillover from above-target headline inflation,” explains Benjamin Reitzes, BMO’s Canadian Rates & Macro Strategist. “One key rationale noted is that the economy no longer needs policy in stimulative territory.”

Bank of Canada Returns To Old Inflation Measure

Despite the finance industry taking away enough to update forecasts, the speech wasn’t meant to set expectations—at least not directly, notes BMO.

“The focus of the speech was the renewal of the inflation targeting framework, and the Governor unveiled that the Bank’s preferred core measures are now CPI-Trim and CPIX,” explains Reitzes.

Neither is a new core measure, but they’re not the headline numbers the media leads with. CPI-Trim seeks to strip out the extremes of the basket, eliminating the top and bottom 20% of price movements. It sounds like that would be a fair trade-off, but in reality, upward price pressure tends to be more extreme than downward. As a result, big price jumps are filtered out with much smaller relative moves downward.

The Governor clarified, however, that these measures will be used in addition to the headline CPI. “Mr. Macklem stressed that the 2% inflation target applies exclusively to headline CPI. The cores will be used as a guide to forecast where overall inflation is headed,” explains Reitzes.


As for CPIX, it stands for Consumer Price Index eXcluding, as it excludes the 8 most volatile components and the effects of indirect tax changes. It’s an oldie that was introduced in 2001, but dropped in 2016 in favour of three core measures—CPI-trim, CPI-median, and CPI-common. A good reminder that sometimes policymakers control inflation, and sometimes they control how it’s measured.

items.content: <p>BMO projects 2% growth for Canada in 2027 as housing markets brace for further rate hikes</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639312262342042131.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: BMO projects 2% growth for Canada in 2027 as housing markets brace for further rate hikes
items.body:
Canada's mortgage markets are heading into 2027 facing at least one more Bank of Canada rate hike, as BMO Capital Markets upgrades its national growth forecast to 2% while identifying British Columbia and Ontario as the provinces most exposed to continued monetary tightening.

The November 24 report by Douglas Porter, CFA, Managing Director and Chief Economist at BMO Capital Markets in Toronto, and Robert Kavcic, Director and Senior Economist at BMO Capital Markets, projects Canada's gross domestic product (GDP) above the 20-year average in 2027.

That follows an estimated 1% expansion in 2026, weighed down by US tariffs of 50% on steel and aluminum and 35% on lumber, with no significant trade resolution assumed in the base case.

"If we do get some kind of arrangement with the US, some certainty, some clarity on trade with the US, I would be much, much more optimistic in 2027, and I think we could grow well above average if we were to get some kind of an arrangement on trade," he said at the event.

On monetary policy, he was equally direct.

"We do believe that the Bank of Canada is likely to hike rates one more time," Porter said. "Our view is that two rate hikes will be enough."

Central banks globally raised rates this year as oil prices drove inflation higher, and Porter flagged that energy product prices — particularly diesel and heating oil — had not yet fully passed through to consumers.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem already signalled the risk of a second-round oil shock and rising December rate odds.

The rate outlook is the most pressing near-term concern for mortgage professionals. Porter outlined the dual pressure on households in a March interview with Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"It's not good. On the one side, there's the hit to confidence because of the uncertainty for the outlook and the very real hit to people's pocketbooks from higher gasoline prices," he said.

"At the same time, we've had this backup in long-term bond yields, which is threatening to push up longer-term mortgage rates. It's tough for the housing market on both fronts."

Experts from the Bank of Canada, Dominion Lending Centres (DLC), and TD Economics say higher rates and inflation remain key factors shaping the outlook for borrowers and the mortgage market in 2027. https://t.co/SP0gdfkLH5 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 23, 2026

Ontario and BC most exposed to further rate hikes

The regional implications for mortgage professionals are significant. Kavcic identified British Columbia and Ontario as the provinces most vulnerable to continued tightening.

"Any upward pressure on mortgage rates would further deter buyers and slow construction activity, delaying a recovery in those markets," he noted in the report, citing elevated household debt and prolonged housing downturns in both provinces.

Ontario prices remain in retreat in some markets and construction has pulled back sharply; BC has endured a multi-year slump.

Regional divide deepens as prairies outperform

Alberta and Saskatchewan are delivering the country's strongest results, backed by elevated oil revenues and minimal US tariff exposure.

An influx of interprovincial residents has reinforced Alberta's consumer spending and residential demand.

Atlantic Canada is also above the national average, driven by migration and public infrastructure investment.

Quebec faces the steepest tariff headwinds, its aluminum sector absorbing a disproportionate share of US trade measures, compounded by its sensitivity to energy price volatility as a manufacturing base.

On the federal budget, Porter was clear about Ottawa's intent. 

"Their priority is really not on reducing the budget deficit — it is on supporting the Canadian economy through this difficult episode of trade uncertainty with the US," he said.

The projected $62.3 billion deficit for the 2026–2027 fiscal year arrives in line with expectations, and BMO estimates that defence and infrastructure commitments could add up to $150 billion to the economy over five years, with domestic suppliers prioritised.

items.description: Record debt and rising delinquency signal growing strain for 2027 mortgage renewals
items.content: <p>Record debt and rising delinquency signal growing strain for 2027 mortgage renewals</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639312227283291504.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Record debt and rising delinquency signal growing strain for 2027 mortgage renewals
items.body:
Canadian households entered the fourth quarter of 2026 carrying record consumer debt, with mounting pressure emerging among mortgage borrowers ahead of what is forecast to be a large renewal year in 2027, according to TransUnion Canada's Q3 2026 Credit Industry Insights Report (CIIR).

Total outstanding consumer credit debt reached $2.66 trillion in Q3 2026, up 3.8% year-over-year. The average Canadian owed $136,024 across all credit products, a 2.9% annual increase.

Mortgages represent 74% of outstanding balances, while non-mortgage debt – including credit cards, auto loans, and lines of credit – grew fastest at 3.6% year-over-year to an average of $28,083 per consumer.

Consumers in the super prime (lowest-risk) credit tier increased 4% year-over-year and represented nearly half of all scored credit-active Canadians.

Bigger balances, not more borrowers

Mortgage debt growth in Q3 2026 was not driven by an expanding pool of borrowers. Between September 2024 and September 2026, the average mortgage balance per consumer rose 8.6%, from $369,658 to $401,509, while the count of active mortgage holders grew by less than 1%.

While delinquency remains below pre-pandemic levels, the concentration of debt in larger individual balances is amplifying the financial stakes at renewal.

Matt Fabian, senior director of financial services research and consulting at TransUnion Canada, said lenders should closely track the divergence.

"Rising debt is being driven by two distinct forces: non-mortgage balance growth has come from an increase in borrowers carrying moderately higher average debt levels, while mortgage balance growth has come from larger balances per borrower as borrower counts have remained flat," Fabian said.

"For lenders, these differing patterns underscore the value of tracking how balances, product mix and payment obligations change over time."

Shaun Cathcart and Garry Bhaura of CREA, Michael Davenport of Oxford Economics, and Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group say higher rates and economic uncertainty are keeping Canada's housing market subdued. https://t.co/3C37E4W4gQ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

Delinquency creep ahead of 2027 renewals

Mortgage delinquency trended upward across all stages in Q3 2026, with balance-level delinquency rising 6 basis points year-over-year and serious delinquency (90-plus days) outpacing account-level increases. That means larger-balance loans are overrepresented among distressed borrowers.

Victor Tran, Rates.ca mortgage and real estate expert, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year that mortgage arrears remain far from crisis territory.

"But I think it's going to be a slow grind," Tran said. "It's not going to be a significant, drastic increase suddenly and I don't think we're going to see sudden mass foreclosures or power of sales."

On October 28, the Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%, its first rate increase since July 2023, adding immediate upward pressure on adjustable-rate mortgages and complicating renewal calculations across a broad segment of the market. 

Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, said that financial pressure on homeowners is real even in the absence of a default crisis.

"Mortgage delinquency is often one of the last signs of financial strain, because most homeowners will cut back in other areas before missing a mortgage payment," she said.

"That's why even a small increase in arrears is worth paying attention to. It can suggest that some households have already used savings, leaned on credit, or reduced everyday spending to keep up. For borrowers coming up for renewal, the question isn't only whether they can make the next payment, but whether payments can be sustained over time."

Fabian added that warning signals typically surface elsewhere in a consumer's finances before a mortgage payment is skipped.

"Rising utilization, growing revolving balances, reduced payments and emerging delinquency on other products can signal weakening financial capacity before a mortgage payment is missed," he said.

"Having a comprehensive view across the consumer wallet can reveal early signs of mortgage stress and give lenders an opportunity to identify risk earlier and engage consumers proactively."
